introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

The paper contains eight questions.
enonce_intro_markdown: A particle of unit mass falls vertically from rest in a resistive medium, where the resistance is proportional to the speed $v$ of the particle. When the particle is moving with speed $u$, the resistive force is equal to half the force of gravity ($g$) on the particle.
incertitudes: Question 7 (ii) : l'énoncé imprimé dit seulement « the particle has covered a distance x = (2u^2/g)(In 4 - 1) » sans préciser l'instant ; le résultat n'est vrai que lorsque la vitesse vaut u (vérifié par le calcul). Le corrigé le dit explicitement. « In4 » est imprimé avec un I majuscule : lu ln 4.
Question 7 (i) : « at time t » figure dans l'énoncé alors que la relation demandée est en fonction de x ; x est la distance parcourue depuis le départ.

questions.enonce_markdown: Show that at time $t$, $v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{v}{2u}\right)$. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $x$ be the distance fallen from the starting point, measured downwards, and $v$ the speed. The forces on the particle (mass $1$) are its weight $g$ downwards and the resistance $R = kv$ upwards ($k$ constant).

**Value of $k$.** When $v = u$ the resistance is half the weight: $ku = \tfrac12 g$, so $k = \dfrac{g}{2u}$.

**Equation of motion** (Newton's second law, downwards positive):

$$1\cdot\frac{dv}{dt} = g - kv = g - \frac{g}{2u}v = g\left(1-\frac{v}{2u}\right).$$

Since $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$,

$$v\frac{dv}{dx} = g\left(1-\frac{v}{2u}\right).$$

(The terminal speed is where the right-hand side is zero, $v=2u$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Show that at time $t$ the particle has covered a distance $x = \dfrac{2u^2}{g}(\ln 4 - 1)$. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Separate the variables in $v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = g\left(1-\dfrac{v}{2u}\right) = \dfrac{g(2u-v)}{2u}$:

$$x = \frac{2u}{g}\int_0^{v}\frac{v}{2u-v}\,dv = \frac{2u}{g}\int_0^{v}\left(-1+\frac{2u}{2u-v}\right)dv$$

$$x = \frac{2u}{g}\Big[-v - 2u\ln(2u-v)\Big]_0^{v} = \frac{2u}{g}\left[-v - 2u\ln\frac{2u-v}{2u}\right].$$

**The stated distance is reached when the speed has become $u$** (the speed used to define the resistance; the printed question does not state this condition, see the note). Putting $v = u$:

$$x = \frac{2u}{g}\left[-u - 2u\ln\frac12\right] = \frac{2u}{g}\big[-u + 2u\ln 2\big] = \frac{2u^2}{g}(2\ln2 - 1)$$

$$x = \frac{2u^2}{g}(\ln 4 - 1).$$

Since $x$ increases strictly with $v$ (the integrand $\frac{v}{2u-v}$ is positive for $0<v<2u$), this distance corresponds to $v=u$ and to no other speed.
